name: Tianwen-1's deployable cameras
short_status: Success: three throwaway cameras, one ejected on the cruise in 2020, one reported released in Mars orbit at the end of 2021, and the one Zhurong dropped on 1 June 2021 for the portrait, still lying in Utopia Planitia.
tagline: CNSA · China · Artefact · 2020 · Multipolar Mars Success
stats: how far south of the landing platform Zhurong drove before releasing the camera
the day the portrait was taken; CNSA published it ten days later
catalogued mass of the camera left on the surface, the only mass figure we could find

facts.label: What CNSA actually said
facts.value: The 11 June 2021 release describes the image it calls 着巡合影, the lander and rover group photo, like this: the rover drove to a point about 10 metres south of the landing platform, released the separation camera installed on the underside of the vehicle, then reversed back to the vicinity of the landing platform. The camera photographed the rover moving and photographed the rover together with the landing platform. The images were sent by wireless signal to the rover, and the rover relayed them to the ground through the orbiter.

facts.label: How the shot was planned
facts.value: CNSA's follow-up release of 27 June 2021 calls the device the WIFI 分离相机, the WiFi separation camera, and explains the choreography. Working from the camera's field of view and focal length, the team planned where the camera would be dropped and what route the rover would drive. The rover went to the separation point, released the camera, reversed to the photo point for a head-on portrait with the landing platform, then turned so that its flank faced the camera for a second, side-on portrait.

facts.label: When it happened
facts.value: 1 June 2021, per the 27 June release. That is ten days after Zhurong rolled off the platform on 22 May and ten days before CNSA unveiled the picture. The same release states that the camera also recorded the rover reversing and turning in place, which CNSA describes as the first time humans obtained imagery of the process of a rover moving on the Martian surface.

facts.label: What the picture shows
facts.value: The landing platform with a Chinese flag on its flank, sitting on flat, rock-strewn ground, with the six-wheeled rover parked beside it and its solar panels spread. Because the camera is on the ground the viewpoint is low, roughly at wheel height, which is why the image reads as a photograph of two objects rather than as engineering documentation.

facts.label: Not the same picture
facts.value: The other widely circulated flag image, 中国印迹 or China's imprint, was not taken by the dropped camera. CNSA's 11 June release says the rover drove to a point about 6 metres from the landing platform in the direction CNSA writes as 东偏南60°, that is 60 degrees south of east, and photographed the platform from there with a camera on the rover itself. The two images are routinely swapped in captions.

facts.label: Where it is
facts.value: The Zhurong landing platform sits at 109.925 E, 25.066 N at an elevation of -4,099.4 m, a position determined from sub-metre images taken by Tianwen-1's own High Resolution Imaging Camera on 2 June 2021 and published by Liu and colleagues. The camera is about 10 metres south of that, which is finer than the published precision of the fix.

facts.label: The only hardware figures we found
facts.value: Jonathan McDowell's deep space catalogue lists the object as Fenli xiangji, ejectable camera, JCAT D01086, released from Zhurong, built by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology (SAST), with a mass of about 1 kg and a box shape roughly 0.1 m on a side. CNSA has published no mass, dimensions, sensor type, resolution, radio specification or battery life for it that we could locate.

facts.label: The first one, in deep space
facts.value: On 1 October 2020, China's National Day, CNSA released images of Tianwen-1 in interplanetary space taken by a small camera the spacecraft had ejected. Spaceflight Now, reporting the release, describes two wide-angle lenses programmed to take one image a second, with the pictures returned to Tianwen-1 over a wireless radio link and downlinked from there. The images show the solar wings, the high-gain dish, the white entry capsule and a red Chinese flag on the side of the cruise stack.

facts.label: The names TDC-1 and TDC-2
facts.value: English Wikipedia and much of the English-language coverage call the two orbiter cameras Tianwen-1 Deployable Camera 1 and 2, and the rover's camera the Tianwen-1 Remote Camera. Those designations are useful and they are what a reader will search for, but we did not find them in any CNSA document. CNSA's own Chinese wording for the rover camera is 分离相机 or WIFI 分离相机, and its 1 October 2020 release calls the orbiter camera a 分离测量传感器, a separation measurement sensor, which is also the name Jonathan McDowell's catalogue gives the two objects it lists as released from the orbiter.

facts.label: The second one, and a gap in the record
facts.value: CNSA's New Year release of 1 January 2022 published four images, the first of them captioned 环绕器与火星合影, the orbiter photographed with Mars, showing the whole orbiter flying above the north polar region with its solar wings and radar antenna deployed. That is a viewpoint only a separated camera can produce. But the release itself, in both its CNSA and its 中国探月工程 versions, describes the picture without saying how it was taken. English sources date the release of a second deployable camera to 31 December 2021; CNSA's own text does not. Chinese press coverage supplies the method but not the date: a press report of 5 January 2022, drawing on the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology team behind the camera, says a separation measurement sensor built by the academy's Institute 803 was again released under ground control and took one picture a second while slowly drifting away from the orbiter, and on 10 February 2022 Xinhua said the New Year pictures were taken by another separation camera.

facts.label: The selfie stick, partly confirmed
facts.value: A second orbiter self-imaging method is widely described: a boom of shape-memory composite, said to weigh 0.8 kg and to extend to 1.6 m, carrying cameras at its tip. English Wikipedia sources that description entirely to posts on a social media account, one of which, dated 30 January 2022, says the boom unfolded by itself when heated after Mars orbit insertion. The builder confirmed part of it: Xinhua, quoting a designer at the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology's Institute 803 on 10 February 2022, says the boom stayed folded through launch and cruise, was heated open from four folded sections after arrival in Mars orbit and reaches up to 1.6 m, and that the picture it took of the orbiter's flag with the Beijing 2022 Olympic and Paralympic emblems reached Earth on the day the Games opened. We found no CNSA or builder statement of the 0.8 kg mass or the shape-memory material, and we do not repeat those as fact.

facts.label: The relay chain
facts.value: CNSA describes the pictures going from the dropped camera to the rover by 无线信号, wireless signal, and from the rover to the ground through the orbiter acting as a relay. Apart from the WiFi in the camera's name in the 27 June release, no frequency, data rate or range has been published in the releases we read. The orbiter had moved into its relay orbit after the landing and was providing communications for the rover.

facts.label: Sound, released the same day
facts.value: The 27 June 2021 release also carried audio: a recording device on Zhurong captured the sound of the rover driving off the landing platform on 22 May 2021. CNSA attributes the sound to the drive mechanism, to the wheels on the ramp and to the wheels on the ground. It does not describe the device as an atmospheric microphone and publishes no specification for it.

facts.label: A Chinese habit, not a one-off
facts.value: Deliberately jettisoning a small camera to photograph your own spacecraft is a technique China has used repeatedly. McDowell's catalogue also records a Chang'e-6 mobile camera, JCAT D01165, carried by the Chang'e-6 lander. The May 2024 date in that catalogue row belongs to the launch. Chang'e-6 landed on the far side on 1 June 2024 UTC and the camera was put down there in early June. The Tianwen-1 cameras are the Mars members of a family.

facts.label: Mission context, as CNSA counted it
facts.value: On 11 June 2021, when the portrait was published, the orbiter was in its relay orbit and Zhurong had worked 28 Martian sols. On 27 June, the orbiter had been flying 338 days, Mars was 360 million km from Earth, and the rover had worked 42 sols and driven 236 m. The last of these releases, published on 1 January 2022, gives figures current to 31 December 2021: the orbiter 526 days in flight, about 350 million km away with a 19.5 minute one-way light time, and Zhurong 225 sols in with 1,400 m on its odometer and about 560 GB of raw science data returned.

facts.label: Timings, in two clocks
facts.value: CNSA publishes in Beijing time, which is UTC plus eight hours. The landing is 15 May 2021 at 07:18 Beijing, which is 14 May at 23:18 UTC. Zhurong drove onto the surface on 22 May; the 10:40 Beijing time usually quoted for that (02:40 UTC) is not in any of the CNSA releases used here, which give only the date. Almost every discrepancy between Chinese and Western accounts of Tianwen-1 dates is this eight-hour offset crossing midnight.

timeline: Tianwen-1 launches from Wenchang on a Long March 5, carrying an orbiter, an entry capsule with a lander and the Zhurong rover, and at least one small camera meant to be thrown away.

A camera is ejected from the cruise stack. Spaceflight Now, reporting the release, has the spacecraft nearing the halfway point of its seven-month journey; no source we found gives the ejection date. Two wide-angle lenses take an image a second and radio the frames back to the spacecraft.
CNSA publishes the deep space self-portrait on China's National Day, showing Tianwen-1 with its solar wings, its dish, the white entry capsule and a red flag, against nothing at all.
Tianwen-1 brakes into Mars orbit, becoming China's first artificial satellite of another planet. It spends three months surveying the landing region from a parking orbit.

23:18 UTC (07:18 on 15 May Beijing): the entry capsule lands in southern Utopia Planitia after about nine minutes of aerodynamic braking, parachute descent, powered hover, hazard avoidance and touchdown.

Zhurong drives down the ramp onto Mars; CNSA gives the date but no time. A recording device on the rover captures the sound of the drive mechanism and the wheels on ramp and ground, released a month later.

The rover drives about 10 m south of the landing platform, releases the WiFi separation camera from under its belly, reverses back towards the platform and stops. The camera photographs it moving, then head-on, then side-on after the rover turns.
Tianwen-1's High Resolution Imaging Camera takes the sub-metre images from orbit that fix the landing site at 109.925 E, 25.066 N, elevation -4,099.4 m.

CNSA unveils the first batch of surface images in Beijing, including the landing site panorama, the terrain image, China's imprint and the lander and rover group photo. The release states that the publication marks the complete success of China's first Mars exploration mission. Zhurong has worked 28 sols.

On the eve of the Communist Party's centenary, CNSA releases the descent footage, the drive-off video and its sound, and the separation camera's own footage of the rover reversing and turning. The rover has driven 236 m in 42 sols.
English-language sources date the release of a second deployable camera in Mars orbit to this day. The CNSA release that carries the resulting images does not mention a camera release.

CNSA's New Year greeting publishes the orbiter photographed above the Martian north polar cap, a close-up of part of the orbiter, the layered north polar ice, and terrain from Zhurong. The orbiter has flown 526 days; the rover has worked 225 sols and driven 1,400 m.

images.caption: The image CNSA publishes as “着巡合影”图, the lander and rover group photo, shot from ground level with the Zhurong rover at the left, solar wings and mast deployed and a red flag on its body, and the landing platform at the right. CNSA's own text states that the rover drove to about 10 m south of the landing platform, released the separation camera mounted on its underside, reversed back towards the platform, and that the camera photographed the rover moving and then the rover and platform together, the frames going by radio to the rover and on to Earth through the orbiter relay.
images.credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

images.caption: The Tianwen-1 cruise stack against empty black space, the white entry capsule at the top, the gold-blanketed orbiter below it with the red Chinese flag on its side, the high-gain dish at the left and a solar wing at the right. CNSA released it on 1 October 2020 and states that the flight image was taken by a 分离测量传感器, a separation measurement sensor, mounted on the outside of the spacecraft and released from it under ground control, using two wide-angle lenses to take one image a second and returning them over a WiFi link.
images.credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

images.caption: The whole Tianwen-1 orbiter seen from outside, flying above the white north polar cap of Mars with its gold body, silver directional antenna, solar wings and radar antenna deployed. CNSA published it in its New Year release of 1 January 2022, identifying the dark region below as Olympia Undae and the bright crater at upper left as Korolev, and describing the polar ice as a mixture of dry ice and water ice. The release describes the scene in detail but does not say how the picture was taken.
images.credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

images.caption: A close view along the flank of the Tianwen-1 orbiter, the gold thermal blanketing and the high-gain dish filling the right of the frame, one solar wing fully deployed at the left, a subsurface radar antenna running parallel to it and the magnetometer boom extending, in CNSA's words, towards the orbiter's upper left, with Mars filling the background. CNSA publishes it in the same 1 January 2022 release as 环绕器局部特写, a close-up of part of the orbiter.
images.credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

images.caption: The image CNSA publishes as “中国印迹”图, China's imprint, showing the Zhurong landing platform alone on the surface with the Chinese flag on its side, its ramps lowered and the rover's wheel tracks curving away across the ground to the right. CNSA's text states it was taken by the rover from about 6 m away in the direction 东偏南 60°, east rotated 60 degrees towards south, so it came from the rover itself and not from the dropped separation camera. CNSA does not name which of the rover's cameras took it.
images.credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)
